newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov widens property tax relief plan to co-ops.
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov widens property tax relief plan to co-ops.

text.p: New York Gov George Pataki on Wednesday switched course and decided to give the owners of cooperative apartments a share in the $3.4 billion property tax savings program he put forward in his budget.

"It is only fair that all New Yorkers who have worked and saved and invested in the American Dream of ownership here in the Empire State are rewarded with lower property taxes -- whether they own homes, condos or co-ops," Pataki said in prepared remarks.

The governor's preliminary budget, which he unveiled in late January, excluded the state's 260,000 cooperative apartments, a decision that fell particularly hard on New York City residents, as it has around 212,000 of the apartments. Another 60,000 Mitchell-Lama co-op units, which are subsidized by the state and city, also would qualify under Pataki's amended program.
A spokesman for Pataki was not immediately available to explain why the governor decided to widen his program, which is designed to lower school property taxes, by adding co-ops.
New York City Council Speaker Peter Vallone, a Democrat, has blasted the governor's property tax relief program for its failure to include co-ops, renters and owners of small buildings.
And the governor's revised plan, included in amendments to his 1998 budget, did not go all the way towards satisfying the New York City official's concerns.

"I am pleased that the governor is responding to my concerns about the inequities to New York City residents. We are now developing strategies that will include all types of households not just those recognized by upstate," Vallone said in prepared comments.

Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver (D-Manhattan) has said he would support an across-the-board cut in property taxes, but had criticized the governor's plan, saying his five-year program would take too long. He said the property tax cuts proposed by the governor were unfair to various areas of the state, estimating they would save Westchester County 2-1/2 times the statewide average. Silver's spokeswoman was not immediately available to comment.
The amount that a New York City resident who owns a co-op or a condominium can expect to save under the governor's new plan was estimated at about $175, up from the initial calculation of $160.

Including the co-ops in the School Tax Relief program would provide another $8 million in property tax savings to senior citizens in the 1997-98 school year, raising the total savings to $118 million in the first year. Taxpayers who are not seniors would get the exemption benefits in the 1998-99 school year.

By the time the program is fully in place in the 2000-01 school year, the governor estimated co-op owners would get about $115 million of tax relief, with about half of this sum going to New York City residents.
